nodes.name: Kart drive physics
nodes.purpose: Per-update integration for every kart on the track: throttle and braking taken from the pad, grip and counter-steer from the surface, gravity and hop launches, angular velocity from the steering ramp, and the final velocity-to-position step.

nodes.name: Engine stat and physics tables
nodes.purpose: One table seeds every kart with 65 handling numbers - gravity, hop impulse, three friction coefficients, free and boosted acceleration, top speed, turning rates and boost ceilings - indexed by engine class, plus the copy loop that stamps them onto a driver when it is created.

nodes.name: Power-slide charge and release
nodes.purpose: The drifting state: the entry condition, the boost meter that fills while the slide is held, the graded release that pays boost back, the steering that is granted inside the slide, and the spin-out that punishes holding it too long.

nodes.name: Boost reserves and flame
nodes.purpose: The reserve pool every boost spends, the speed ceiling a boost raises, the flame model size that reports the payout, and the per-update drain that returns the kart to its class top speed.

nodes.name: Surface and terrain grip
nodes.purpose: The table that turns a level surface type into grip, counter-steer ratio, a speed cap for loose ground and the particle set for the tyres, plus the guarded lookups the kart physics calls every update.

nodes.name: Quadblock collision search
nodes.purpose: How the world mesh answers a moving sphere: bounding-box rejection against the level collision blocks, low and high detail triangle split, and the sweeping search the kart runs each update to find the ground it stands on and the walls it scrapes.

nodes.name: Chase camera
nodes.purpose: Places the third-person camera behind the kart: heading offset, pull-back distance derived from speed, height above the chassis, the reverse view, the look-down when the kart is hit, and the slow spin-around shot.

nodes.name: Opponent driving
nodes.purpose: Computer drivers follow a baked navigation path: one of three path slots per level is loaded, a heading is derived by comparing kart position with the next node, and contact between two computer karts is resolved by rank.

nodes.name: Weapons and damage states
nodes.purpose: Projectiles and thrown hazards: which victim a homing shot picks, how a hit is routed to the kart, and the timed states - spin, blast, shield hold - a kart enters before it regains control of its own physics.

cards.name: Class top speed per engine
cards.summary: The shared physics table holds a column per engine class, and each class gets its own top speed and speedometer scale; the numbers are stored in 256ths of a kilometre per hour.
cards.behavior: Every kart is stamped with a 65-entry block of handling numbers at creation, and the entry holding top speed differs per engine class. The block carries five columns even though the retail build only exposes four of them. Speed is carried as an integer where 256 units equal one kilometre per hour, so the fastest class tops out a little over 54 km/h while the slowest sits near 50 km/h. A separate entry scales the speedometer and is larger than the class top speed for every engine, so the needle has headroom it only uses while a boost is being spent. The speed resolver finally clamps the sum of class speed, collected-fruit bonus and boost bonus, so stacking every source cannot push a kart far past the fastest class.

constants.unit: internal speed units, where 256 units are one kilometre per hour; evaluated on every update at 30 Hz (one update is 32 ms)

cards.name: Acceleration curve
cards.summary: Throttle does not add a fixed force: free acceleration is a per-class value, spending a boost swaps in a much larger one, and standing on a boost surface substitutes a single large constant instead.
cards.behavior: Each update the drive step decides which of three accelerations to use. While the kart is on a boost surface the drive step branches to one large constant and gives up on the gentle curve, so speed climbs as fast as the cap allows. Otherwise the class acceleration value is used, and while a boost is being spent it is replaced by a value a little over twice as large. A surface that limits top speed scales the acceleration down proportionally, which is why loose ground feels sluggish rather than merely slow. The chosen acceleration is multiplied by the milliseconds that elapsed since the previous update and shifted down five places, so a frame that takes twice as long adds twice the speed instead of the same amount. The resulting delta is projected onto the kart heading and added to the velocity vector. A friction term then removes the part of the velocity magnitude that exceeds the signed base speed, capped at the acceleration this frame granted, which is what makes a kart coast back down once the throttle is released.

constants.name: Free acceleration, engine 0
constants.unit: internal speed units per update at 30 Hz, scaled by elapsed milliseconds over 32

cards.name: Hop impulse and gravity
cards.summary: A hop is a single vertical impulse added on the first update of the jump, after which gravity is the only vertical force; both are constants per engine class, and one flag on the block underneath scales gravity down.
cards.behavior: Pressing the hop button does not start an animation that carries the kart upward - it hands the kart one upward velocity value on the first update and then gets out of the way. Every update afterwards subtracts a gravity constant from the vertical velocity, and that subtraction is scaled by elapsed milliseconds so a slow frame falls further. Blocks flagged for reduced gravity replace the constant with a fraction of it, which is how the floaty sections of a track are authored without touching the kart. A scripted or hazard-driven hop is expressed as a multiple of the same impulse, so a forced launch of three times the normal strength uses the identical code path. Horizontal speed is untouched by the hop: only the vertical component of the velocity vector changes, which keeps the line the kart takes through the air predictable.

constants.name: Hop impulse
constants.unit: internal velocity units in 8.8 fixed point, so 256 units move the kart one world unit per update; added once per update at 30 Hz; written into the vertical velocity on the first update of the hop only

constants.name: Downward acceleration
constants.unit: internal velocity units subtracted from vertical velocity per update at 30 Hz, scaled by elapsed milliseconds over 32

constants.name: Reduced-gravity surface scale
constants.unit: percent of the normal gravity constant, applied on every update while the kart rests on a low-gravity surface

constants.name: Gravity fraction denominator
constants.unit: percent, the denominator of the reduced-gravity fraction; evaluated on every update at 30 Hz

constants.name: Forced hop multiplier
constants.unit: multiple of the hop impulse, applied once on the update a forced hop begins

cards.name: Ramp launch from surface normals
cards.summary: Driving off a sloped face converts forward speed into upward speed by projecting the velocity onto the triangle normal, so a flat face launches nothing and a steep face launches hard.
cards.behavior: When a kart leaves the ground the engine looks at the normal of the triangle it just left and asks how much of the kart horizontal velocity points along that normal. A face with no horizontal gradient has a vertical normal only, the projection collapses to zero, and the kart simply falls. A face tilted along the direction of travel returns a large positive number, and dividing that by the vertical component of the normal turns it into an upward velocity in the same units as the rest of the physics. Faces so nearly flat that the projected value is under a small threshold are treated as flat, which stops the kart from being nudged upward by seams between blocks. The larger of that ramp projection and the surface-normal jump projection is then combined with the hop impulse in quadrature, so hopping just before a ramp adds to the launch instead of discarding it. A per-level ceiling caps the launch and can be raised or lowered by the level, and the vertical velocity is clamped upward to the chosen value rather than added to.

constants.name: Minimum normal tilt that launches
constants.unit: units of the surface normal vertical component; compared on the update the kart leaves the face

constants.name: Default launch ceiling
constants.unit: internal vertical velocity units, applied once on the update of the launch when the level does not override it

constants.name: Maximum launch ceiling
constants.unit: internal vertical velocity units, the upper bound a level may author; applied once on the update of the launch

cards.name: Steering rate ramp
cards.summary: Steering is an angular velocity that ramps up over a handful of frames, holds briefly, then decays; the class turn stat sets the ceiling and the surface friction scales how fast it is reached.
cards.behavior: Holding a direction does not snap the kart to a turn rate. The requested rate from the stick is scaled by the class turn stat and by the turning multiplier, then the current angular rate is moved toward it in fixed steps whose size comes from the class turn-input delay and the surface friction. Steering is therefore slower to bite on low-grip ground even though the ceiling is the same. A separate ramp modulates how much steering authority has been granted since the stick went over: it climbs across the first few frames, holds through a short plateau, then falls away over a longer window, which is what makes a quick tap feel sharp and a long hold feel stable. Once the window has passed the ramp contributes nothing and the angular rate simply stays where it is. Braking and accelerating together halves the rate ceiling and lengthens the steps, so a kart cannot be steered as tightly under combined input.

cards.name: Velocity from heading and counter-steer
cards.summary: A single signed speed plus two angles becomes a three-dimensional velocity vector each update, and a lateral acceleration derived from the surface ratio pushes back against the direction the kart is turning.
cards.behavior: The kart keeps one scalar speed rather than a free 3D vector. Each update that scalar is multiplied by the sine and cosine of the yaw angle to get a horizontal component, which is then split again by the sine and cosine of the pitch, producing the three world-space velocity terms. Because the scalar is signed, reversing simply flips every component at once. Alongside that, a counter-steer force is computed from the difference between the current and previous steering angle, clamped to a per-kart limit and looked up through a sine table, then scaled by the surface counter-steer ratio and a small negative strength constant. The force is rotated into world space and added to the acceleration buffer, so a hard surface pushes back harder than a slippery one and a ratio of zero disables the effect entirely. The effect is skipped below a small speed, while warping, while crashed and while the chassis is not touching ground, which keeps it out of the recovery states.

constants.name: Counter-steer strength
constants.unit: internal acceleration units in 8.8 fixed point per unit of surface ratio, added on every 30 Hz update

constants.name: Counter-steer dead zone
constants.unit: kilometres per hour, held in 256ths internally; tested on every 30 Hz update

constants.name: Counter-steer ratio, plain road
constants.unit: 8.8 fixed-point surface ratio where 256 is full strength and 0 disables the effect, consumed on every update at 30 Hz

constants.name: Counter-steer ratio, ice
constants.unit: 8.8 fixed-point surface ratio where 256 is full strength and 0 disables the effect, consumed on every update at 30 Hz

cards.name: Power-slide charge and graded release
cards.summary: Holding a hop button through a hard turn starts a slide with a fixed-length boost meter; the meter fills with elapsed time, and releasing it in the last half second pays boost in up to three chained steps.
cards.behavior: A slide begins when the stick is far enough over, the hop button is down, the kart is off the brake and the speed is above half the class top speed. The slide installs its own set of update and angle functions, resets a boost meter to full length and starts two counters recording how long the slide has run. While the button is held the meter drains with elapsed milliseconds; when it reaches empty a chime fires and the driver is locked out of any further charge until the button is released. Releasing while the meter is in its last stretch converts the remaining length into reserves through a linear map, so releasing exactly as the meter empties gives the largest payout and releasing early gives less. The payout also scales with how many chained boosts have already been taken in the same slide, and each chain step raises the flame level used for the effect, up to three in a row. Releasing while the meter is still in its green stretch gives nothing but a small visual reset. Once the reserves are granted the flame persists for a fixed slice of elapsed time rather than a fixed number of frames.

constants.name: Boost meter length
constants.unit: meter units of 32 ms each, so a full bar takes one second of sliding at 30 Hz

constants.name: Release window length
constants.unit: meter units of 32 ms each at 30 Hz, measured back from the empty end; the graded release region

constants.name: Chained boosts per slide
constants.unit: boosts, counted on every 30 Hz update while the slide is held

constants.name: Flame level step per chain
constants.unit: left shift applied to the chain counter when the boost fires; evaluated on the update of the release at 30 Hz

constants.name: Chained flame persistence
constants.unit: multiples of 32 ms, so about 480 ms of flame at 30 Hz

constants.name: Meter storage shift
constants.unit: left shift converting meter units to 32 ms ticks; applied once when the slide starts

constants.name: Slide entry speed floor
constants.unit: halving shift applied to the class top speed, sampled on every 30 Hz update

cards.name: Drift angle and spin-out limit
cards.summary: A slide is also a steering resource: the longer it is held the more steering is granted, and holding it past a fixed count of updates spins the kart out and takes the controls away.
cards.behavior: Inside a slide the angular rate is built from two parts: a mapped term that grows with time spent sliding and rewards the driver with sharper turning, plus a term from the stick that is scaled by one of two different steering speeds depending on whether the stick agrees or disagrees with the slide direction. That second term is what makes leaning into a slide different from fighting it. A counter records how long the slide has been held in the current direction; swinging to the other side runs it back toward zero before it starts accumulating on the other sign, and with no stick input it is interpolated back to neutral one unit at a time. The moment the counter passes the class drift limit the controls are locked out and a spin state takes over, and swinging the other way past the negative of the same limit does the same, so a switchback slide has its own budget. Past half the limit the game starts a near-spin warning: a small oscillating offset is added to the kart heading and the tyres make noise, which is the cue to release. Slide time is also capped so the steering reward saturates rather than growing without bound.

constants.name: Slide updates before spin-out
constants.unit: updates at 30 Hz, so two seconds of continuous sliding in one direction

constants.name: Slide time cap
constants.unit: multiples of 32 ms, so the steering reward saturates after about 1.9 seconds of slide time at 30 Hz

constants.name: Near-spin warning point
constants.unit: right shift applied to the slide limit, so the warning begins at half the spin-out count; checked on every 30 Hz update

constants.name: Spin-out control lockout
constants.unit: internal ticks, 32 of which pass per 30 Hz update, so 960 ticks is one second; ~1 second of no steering input at 30 Hz

constants.name: Drift boost pitch rate
constants.unit: multiples of elapsed milliseconds over 32, added to the kart pitch axis on every update at 30 Hz while a drift boost is alive

constants.name: Slide camera spin rate

cards.name: Reserve pool and flame payout
cards.summary: Every boost in the game writes into the same reserve pool and raises the same speed ceiling in fixed steps; the flame model size reports which step was reached and the pool drains with elapsed time.
cards.behavior: A boost is not a fixed-duration state. It adds a quantity of reserve and raises a speed ceiling that lasts until the reserve runs out, which is why a long slide chain or a boost pad followed by another pad stacks so well. The ceiling is built from a base single-boost value plus eight units per flame level, so the payout is graded rather than binary. The flame model is chosen from the flame level with a size floor of four and a ceiling of eight, so the visual is clamped while the arithmetic is not. Reserves are decremented by the elapsed milliseconds of each update, and when they reach nothing the speed ceiling is recomputed back down to the class value, which is what produces the gentle fall back to normal speed. Boosts that come from a pad top up an outside timer instead of the reserve pool, so sitting on a pad keeps the effect alive frame by frame instead of stacking a single large amount.

constants.name: Speed added per flame level

constants.name: Flame model size ceiling

cards.name: Surface grip and speed caps
cards.summary: Each surface type carries its own steering friction, an optional top-speed cap, a counter-steer ratio and its tyre particles, and the kart reads the record for the block it is standing on every update.
cards.behavior: The physics never asks what a surface looks like, only for a record indexed by a small surface id. That record holds a friction value where 256 is neutral, a speed cap the kart is dragged down to on loose ground, a counter-steer ratio used by the lateral force, a lean multiplier for the drift camera and two particle emitters for the tyres. Plain road, stone and hardpack all use neutral friction and no cap, so on those the surface alone never changes how the kart feels. Ice is the outlier: friction falls to an eighth, so every steering step taken on it is an eighth of the normal one, the speed cap drops, and the lean multiplier is halved on top. Loose ground such as dirt and mud works the other way and keeps full friction while capping the speed, which is why a kart there crawls instead of sliding. Mud also sinks the chassis: the force step clamps the vertical velocity so the kart settles toward a floor instead of falling through it. A separate short table describes what happens on contact with a wall or a soft obstacle, and both lookups fall back to the first entry when handed an unknown id.

constants.unit: 8.8 fixed-point multiplier where 256 is neutral, scaling the steering-rate step on every update at 30 Hz

constants.name: Dirt speed cap
constants.unit: internal speed units, where 256 units are one kilometre per hour; evaluated on every update at 30 Hz (one update is 32 ms); the kart is held at or below this while in contact, checked every 30 Hz update

constants.name: Ice steering friction
constants.unit: 8.8 fixed-point multiplier where 256 is neutral, scaling the steering-rate step on every update at 30 Hz

cards.name: Chassis collision sphere and triangle split
cards.summary: The kart is a sphere of a fixed radius swept through the level mesh; the search rejects blocks by bounding box, then splits each candidate into two or eight triangles depending on how many players are on screen.
cards.behavior: Collision starts from a sphere around the chassis with a radius chosen to fit the kart, and the same radius is handed both to the generic search and to the block search so the two never disagree. A block is skipped outright unless its bounding box overlaps the sphere box on all three axes, which removes almost the entire mesh before any triangle maths runs. Candidates are then split differently by player count: with one or two players each block is split into eight triangles for a fine-grained normal, while with three or four players only two triangles are used, trading shape accuracy for the extra cars on screen. A flat quad is tested once as two triangles, but a block whose fourth vertex differs is tested as two halves so the fold is respected. Triangle tests are skipped unless the block carries one of the wanted layer bits and none of the ignored ones, which is how a search asks for ground only, walls only, or both.

constants.name: Chassis collision radius
constants.unit: world units; swept and re-tested on every 30 Hz update

constants.name: Wanted block layers
constants.unit: bit mask of the ground and wall layers, tested on every block examined each 30 Hz update

constants.name: Player count that switches to coarse blocks
constants.unit: karts on screen; the detail level is chosen once per update at 30 Hz

constants.name: Coarse triangles per block

cards.name: Chase camera framing
cards.summary: The camera hangs behind the kart at a distance mapped from speed, rises a fixed height above it, and adds a half-turn offset plus the kart yaw; holding the rear-view button flips that offset by the same half turn.
cards.behavior: Framing is built from three numbers: a yaw that follows the kart heading with a fixed half-turn offset, a distance that the engine maps from the smoothed camera speed into a range between a near and a far value, and a height above the chassis. As the kart speeds up the camera is pulled back until the distance saturates, and it eases back in when the kart slows, so the framing breathes with the race instead of snapping. The pitch is nudged downward when the kart is undamaged and back to level while it is in a hit state, which is what gives a clean chase view normally and a looser view when the driver has lost control. Boost stretches the pull-back briefly and then decays, giving the sensation of acceleration without a permanent zoom-out. A transition between camera modes sets a destination and blends toward it over a full second, and the rear-view button simply adds the same half-turn used for the forward offset so the camera swings all the way around. A separate shot orbits the kart on a sine and cosine pair at a fixed radius, used when the race wants to show the kart from every side.

cards.name: Opponent path following
cards.summary: Computer drivers do not steer by feel: they read a baked chain of navigation nodes, compare their position with the next node and turn toward the heading that difference implies.
cards.behavior: Each level supplies navigation paths in three slots, selected by an index, stored as a header plus an array of nodes. The header carries a count and a validity tag, and the loader checks the tag before trusting the count so an out-of-date path silently collapses to zero nodes instead of walking off the end of a stale array. A driver tracks its position in 8.8 fixed point and shifts it down to whole world units before comparing with the node position, so the comparison happens in whole world units, where squared distances stay small. The heading between kart and node is built from the horizontal distance and the height difference, converted to a rotation, and then offset by a half turn to point the model the other way. Two computer karts in contact are separated using race rank to decide which one is treated as the leader rather than using momentum, which keeps a pack of them from locking together.

constants.name: Position fixed-point shift
constants.unit: right shift turning 8.8 fixed-point world coordinates into whole world units; applied on every 30 Hz update

constants.name: Heading angle scale
constants.unit: vertical exaggeration factor in the heading lookup, evaluated once per 30 Hz update

constants.name: Heading half-turn offset
constants.unit: angular units in 4096-per-turn scale, applied once per 30 Hz update when the node heading is stored

constants.name: Navigation path slots
constants.unit: paths per level, one per route; resolved once when the level loads

constants.name: Path validity tag
constants.unit: sentinel compared once when the path is loaded; a mismatch zeroes the node count rather than reading stale data

cards.name: Hits, lockouts and shields
cards.summary: A weapon hit is routed through one entry point that refuses to touch an invulnerable or shielded kart, and otherwise installs a state whose control lockout is a different length for each damage kind.
cards.behavior: Every hazard funnels its hit through the same state picker, which first checks whether the victim is already holding a protective effect or has temporary invulnerability and, if so, plays a taunt and returns without changing anything. A held shield is not a separate code path - it is consumed inside the same function, granting a longer invulnerability window and popping the bubble before the hit is discarded. Each damage kind then maps to a concrete state and a lockout length: a spin costs about a second of control, a blast costs about two and a half seconds and hands the kart to a tumbling state, and lighter kinds return without touching the state at all. The lockout is stored in a timer that the drive step decrements by elapsed milliseconds, which is why a kart hit on a slow frame recovers on roughly the same clock time as one hit on a fast frame. Thrown hazards carry their own short cooldown after release so a dropped object does not immediately re-arm and hit the kart that dropped it.

constants.name: Spin-out lockout
constants.unit: internal ticks, 32 of which pass per 30 Hz update, so 960 ticks is one second; about one second of no input at 30 Hz

constants.name: Blast lockout
constants.unit: internal ticks, 32 of which pass per 30 Hz update, so 960 ticks is one second; about two and a half seconds of no input at 30 Hz

constants.name: Shield invulnerability window
constants.unit: internal ticks, 32 of which pass per 30 Hz update, so 960 ticks is one second; granted on the update the shield absorbs a hit

constants.name: Thrown hazard cooldown
constants.unit: internal ticks, 32 of which pass per 30 Hz update, so 960 ticks is one second; counted down by elapsed milliseconds on every 30 Hz update

constants.name: Stronger boost item fruit threshold

cards.name: Homing target selection
cards.summary: A homing shot reserves a slot in a fixed global budget, picks the victim by the smallest planar distance among its own projectiles, and clears the on-screen target marker when it detonates.
cards.behavior: Firing a homing projectile first checks a global counter and refuses outright once a fixed number are already in flight, which caps how many tracking objects the engine will ever simulate at once. The victim is whatever the aim step picked rather than the race leader, so the launch stores that driver as the projectile target and the projectile never re-picks. Every projectile that shares a target compares itself against the others using the squared horizontal distance between the projectile and its target, so no square root is taken during the search and the comparison is monotonic. The winner is the one closest on the ground plane, and the height difference is deliberately ignored so a projectile cannot be ignored simply because it has been thrown high. On impact the projectile kills its own thread, mutes its flight audio and clears the marker that was drawn on the victim screen, so the target display is clean again as soon as the shot lands.
